title: Common Property Frauds in India: Six Warning Signs
excerpt: Learn six common fraud risks property buyers should investigate before paying or registering a property.
content:
Property buyers should not rely only on appearances, verbal assurances, possession, registration, or photocopied documents. Verification must be appropriate to the specific property, parties and transaction.

1. Fake Ownership
A person may offer a property without being its lawful owner or may rely on forged or manipulated documents. Verify the seller’s identity, authority and chain of title independently.

2. Double Sale Fraud
The same property may be promised or sold to multiple buyers. Review prior agreements, registrations, possession claims and relevant transaction records.

3. Hidden Mortgage
A property may already secure a loan or debt that the seller has not disclosed. Enquire into mortgages, charges, original documents and relevant registry information.

4. Family or Inheritance Disputes
Other legal heirs or family members may assert ownership or challenge the seller’s authority. Succession history and the rights of relevant parties require review.

5. Unapproved Construction
A building may lack a sanctioned plan, completion approval or permission for its actual construction or use. Compare municipal approvals with the site.

6. Fake Power of Attorney
A fraudulent, revoked, limited or ineffective power of attorney may be used to claim authority to sell. Verify the instrument, principal, continuing validity and powers granted.

Precautions Before Paying
Verify identity, ownership and authority independently. Inspect original documents. Review title history, mortgages, charges, litigation, sanctioned plans, taxes, possession and the property description. Record material representations and use qualified professionals appropriate to the transaction.

Important: This is general educational information, not a title certificate or legal opinion for a particular property.

title: How Banks Verify Property Before Giving a Home Loan
excerpt: Understand the legal, technical and document checks banks generally conduct before approving a home loan—and why buyers still need independent due diligence.
content:
A home loan is not approved only on the borrower’s income and credit profile. Before financing a property, a bank generally conducts legal and technical checks to assess whether the property is acceptable as security. The exact process and documents may vary by lender, property type and location.

1. Title Verification
The bank’s empanelled lawyer generally examines ownership documents and the chain of title, often covering the previous 20 to 30 years where records permit. The review may identify breaks in ownership, inconsistent descriptions, missing transfers or questions about the seller’s authority.

2. Encumbrance Check
The bank may review an encumbrance certificate, registration records and other relevant information to identify an existing mortgage, charge, attachment, agreement or legal liability affecting the property. An encumbrance certificate alone may not reveal every risk, so supporting records and original documents remain important.

3. Approved Building Plan
For a constructed property, the sanctioned building plan and relevant municipal approvals are normally examined. The actual construction should be compared with the approved plan to identify unauthorised additions, deviations or an impermissible use.

4. Technical Valuation
An engineer or valuer may inspect the property to assess its location, measurements, physical condition, stage of construction and reasonable market value. The bank may base the eligible loan amount on its assessed value rather than only on the sale price agreed between buyer and seller.

5. RERA Compliance for New Projects
Where the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act applies, the bank may check the project’s RERA registration, promoter details, disclosed approvals and other project information. Buyers should independently compare the promoter’s representations with the information available on the relevant RERA portal.

6. Legal Heir and Chain Documents
If ownership arose through inheritance, gift, partition, settlement or another family arrangement, the bank may ask for succession and supporting chain documents. The rights of legal heirs, co-owners and other interested persons must be examined before accepting the property as security.

7. Litigation Search
The legal review may include searches for pending court cases, attachments, acquisition proceedings or other disputes concerning the property or parties. Search coverage can be limited by record availability, spelling variations and the information supplied for verification.

Why Independent Due Diligence Still Matters
A bank’s verification is primarily undertaken for the lender’s credit and security assessment. It is not a guarantee that the buyer will receive an undisputed title or that every fraud, mortgage, claim, approval issue or litigation will be discovered. The buyer should appoint an independent property lawyer, inspect original documents, verify the seller’s identity and authority, review relevant public records and obtain transaction-specific advice before paying a substantial amount or signing documents.

Important: This article provides general educational information. Verification requirements vary, and it is not a legal opinion, title certificate or assurance concerning any particular property or loan.
